email.scenario: Your amateur theater group hired a set of period costumes from Harlow Costume Hire for last week's production. After the final night, while packing up, you found that the lining of one hired coat had been torn: its sleeve caught on a nail backstage during a quick scene change. The costumes are due back at the workshop soon, and you have never met the wardrobe keeper who looks after them.
email.subject: Damage to a hired coat
bullets: Apologize for the torn lining of the hired coat.
Explain how the coat was damaged backstage.
Propose a solution for getting the lining repaired, such as paying for a tailor's repair or returning the coat with the other costumes for the workshop to mend.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: This week we are looking at how bus operators collect fares. On most regional buses, every rider boards at the front door and shows a ticket to the driver. Some operators have instead opened every door for boarding and rely on inspectors who check tickets at random during the journey. Should a regional bus operator let riders board through every door and rely on random ticket inspections? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Mireille
studentPosts.post: I think every door should be open. On my route the bus loses a minute or two at each busy stop while people queue at the front, and by the end of the line it is always late. A bus that keeps to its timetable attracts more riders, which matters more than catching a few cheats.

studentPosts.name: Tobias
studentPosts.post: I disagree. When the driver sees every ticket, almost nobody travels without paying. Inspectors can only cover a few buses a day, so plenty of riders will take the risk, and a regional operator with thin fare income cannot afford that. Honest passengers would end up paying higher fares to cover the loss.
